content:
Earlier this year, Apple decided to completely discontinue its Pro Display XDR. While it was an outstanding piece of hardware, it hadn't been updated in years and still cost upwards of $6,000. Their new lineup consists of the Studio Display and the all-new Studio Display XDR, both of which are excellent in their own right, but now only available with a 27-inch 5K screen. The XDR starts at a hefty $3,299, and can be configured up to $3,600 before tax. This left a gap in the market for a larger, retina-class display for Mac users, and that's exactly what the new Meirro Pro fills. The Meirro Pro is a 32-inch 6K display built with an all-aluminium chassis. It supports single-cable connectivity, comes with an adjustable stand, and costs just $1,199. I've been using it as my primary display, and while Meirro made some trade-offs to hit that price point, it might be the most compelling Studio Display alternative I've tested. Here's everything you need to know.

Be sure to check out our hands-on video with the Meirro Pro to see it in action!

Design and Specifications

The first thing you'll notice is how remarkably similar it looks to the existing Apple Studio Display. It blends naturally into any Apple setup without missing a beat. It's fully CNC-machined aluminium with a colour-matched adjustable stand, and it feels incredibly premium. The build quality of this display inspires confidence in any setup. Most non-Apple displays on the market use plastic housings and stands that are flimsier than you'd think, but there's not a bit of plastic to be found anywhere on the Meirro Pro.

The unboxing and setup process for this display is also incredibly simple. You just attach the base to the stand, then mount the stand to the back of the display, plug it in, and you're good to go. The design is about as minimal as it gets, with no buttons whatsoever, and the power supply is built right into the display. This means no ugly brick dangling from the power cable, keeping your desk as clean as possible. It also ships with both an adjustable stand and a VESA mount in the box at no extra cost. Again, this is a very Apple-esque product, and exactly what I was looking for.

But now, let's get back to how the actual display performs. As I mentioned at the beginning, this is a true 6K panel. It's a 32-inch Nano IPS Black panel with a resolution of 6144 × 3456, which translates to 224 ppi, giving you retina-level sharpness. Here are the key specs to note:

  • 32-inch Nano IPS Black panel
  • 6144 × 3456 resolution
  • 224 PPI
  • 60Hz refresh rate
  • 2,000:1 contrast ratio
  • 10-bit colour supporting over 1.07 billion colours
  • 98% DCI-P3 colour gamut coverage
  • 99.5% Adobe RGB colour gamut coverage
  • Typical brightness of 450 nits, with HDR peak brightness of 750 nits

The panel also uses a glossy anti-reflective coating as the only display option. While I would have liked to have a matte option available, the glossy coating still performs quite well even in a room with plenty of windows.

Port Selection and Accessories

Similar to Apple's display offerings, the Meirro Pro also keeps things minimal, with just five USB-C ports on the back serving as the only inputs and outputs. One of these ports acts as the primary upstream connection, supporting DisplayPort 2.1 with up to 80Gbps of bandwidth, and delivering up to 96W of power delivery to keep your MacBook charged at all times. This means you only need a single cable to carry your 6K signal. The remaining four USB-C ports are downstream, but since they're USB 2.0, data transfer speeds are quite limited. However, they're perfectly adequate for webcams, speakers, and other peripherals.

Since the Meirro Pro has no buttons whatsoever (not even a power button), a remote very similar to the previous-generation Apple TV remote is included in the box. It features a power button and lets you access the display's system settings whenever you need to.

My Experience and Setup

I've been using the Meirro Pro as the only display on my desk, and the experience has been fantastic. The 32-inch size combined with the 6K resolution gives me both the physical real estate and pixel density I need from a high-end Mac display.

My setup is fairly straightforward. I personally use external SSDs all the time and like using the Satechi Thunderbolt hub, so I run the display through that hub. One Thunderbolt cable goes from the display to my hub, and another Thunderbolt cable goes from my hub to my MacBook Pro. Everything works just as smoothly as you'd expect.

I've thrown everything from my daily workflow at this display, and it's handled it all with ease. I've edited timelines in Final Cut Pro and organised all my media, and the extra screen real estate really does help. I also spend most of my work day researching, which often means having a ton of tabs and windows open at once, and the extra pixel density makes it feel even larger than 32 inches. The most important spec for this display is its 224 PPI. It allows macOS, and even iPadOS, to scale exactly as Apple intended.

The last thing I want to mention is that the build quality really does help reduce wobble. Most displays of this kind wobble around when you type at your desk, especially when you're using a standing desk (which I am). So the combination of build quality and a solid stand effectively cuts down on that wobble. Whether you're looking at the specs or actually using it, the Meirro Pro has more than proven itself worthy as a Studio Display replacement. But at this price point, there are still some trade-offs to discuss.

Trade-offs

Again, a 32-inch 6K display made of CNC aluminium for under $1,200 almost sounds too good to be true. Meirro had to make some decisions to get the price down to this level. Since most potential buyers will be comparing it to the Studio Display, it's worth pointing out what those trade-offs are. The Meirro Pro does not have or support the following:

  • No built-in webcam
  • No speakers
  • No microphone
  • No support for daisy-chaining

Personally, these trade-offs are worth the cost savings since I already have an external webcam and speakers. The lack of a microphone doesn't bother me either, as I use AirPods or a Shure microphone when I need to. But I still want everyone to know this information so anyone considering this display can be aware.

The last trade-off I noticed is the speed of the USB-C ports on the back of the display. Apple's Studio Display offers a total of four USB-C ports, two of which are Thunderbolt, and two of which are USB 3.0 speeds. The Meirro Pro, while offering more USB-C ports, only has one that is Thunderbolt, with the remaining four being the much slower USB 2.0 spec. Again, this doesn't impact me much since I have the Satechi Thunderbolt dock, but I can understand other users' need for faster ports.

But even with these trade-offs considered, I still think this is a no-brainer recommendation over Apple's Studio Display because of the sheer value the Meirro Pro delivers.

Pricing and Availability

The Meirro Pro normally retails for $1,299 but is currently available for pre-order at $1,199. Shipping is expected to begin on August 1st. In theory, if you already have a display arm, you can opt out of the included stand to save $50, bringing the total down to $1,149. That $1,199 price includes:

  • Meirro Pro Display
  • Aluminium Stand
  • VESA Mount
  • USB-C Cable
  • Power Cable
  • Remote

Wrap-up

The Meirro Pro is the best true Studio Display alternative I've tested. For $1,199, you get a 32-inch 6K display with retina-level sharpness, a glossy Nano IPS Black panel, an all-aluminium build, single-cable Mac connectivity, an adjustable stand, and a VESA mount. If you're looking for the most complete, all-in-one Apple desktop experience, the Studio Display still has its merits; but if you already have some external accessories and truly value screen size, resolution, build quality, and value, the Meirro Pro is an easy recommendation.

What do you think? Is this a display you'd consider picking up? Do you already own a Studio Display? Will you miss the Pro Display XDR? I'd love to know your thoughts. Again, be sure to check out our video to see it in action!
